newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold-Low prices fail to shake summer stupor.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold-Low prices fail to shake summer stupor.

text.p: Asian gold demand remains in a seasonal slump, failing to be revived by a recent steep drop in world prices, bullion traders said on Friday.
Hong Kong premiums edged up to around U.S. 80 cents over the spot London price, from U.S. 60 cents at the beginning of the week, largely on short-covering, dealers said.
"Now gold is higher, there is little physical interest," said one Hong Kong source, noting the summer months of June, July and August were traditionally slow.
"We had some good demand yesterday when gold traded at US$339 per ounce and below, with some bargain-hunting interest from the physical side," said one dealer.
Spot gold was trading at $339.60/340.10 per ounce at 0328 GMT, with little physical activity seen in the market, dealers said.
Hong Kong spot gold opened at $339.70/340.20 an ounce on Friday, slightly lower than New York's Thursday close at $340.20/70 an ounce.
Gold would remain locked in a range between $338 and $343 an ounce over the next week, dealers said.

Overall, Asia's physical gold demand was slow and was expected to stay soft over the next week or so even though New York gold on Wednesday ended quoted at $338.90/40 per ounce, approaching four-year lows of around $336.15 per ounce, Singapore precious metal dealers said.
News earlier this week of the Belgian central bank's plan to sell gold to make commemorative coins has added to downward pressure on prices.
"This piece of news from Belgium served as a catalyst in the market," one bank trader in Singapore said. "It was used as an excuse to bring the market down."
Traders said heavy producer selling, especially by Australia, had built up to the point that the Belgian report became the trigger for gold prices in the market to plunge.
But Asian demand had not picked up substantially despite the falling prices
"Some European houses were calling up and asking how's physical demand. And I told them 'Sorry, it's not there.' In fact, the Indian market is very slow as well," another bank dealer said.

"India is buying some bits, but the real demand won't show up until the last four months of the year. It's simply not the merry months," a retailer in Singapore said. "Retail buying is stagnant. Demand is very weak."
The poor offtake had hit gold premiums in the city-state.
Singapore premiums eased slightly to 68-70 U.S. cents over spot London prices from last week's 70-75 cents, traders said.
"The premiums cannot creep up because demand is not there," a dealer said.
Premiums in Singapore have slipped from a peak in the first two months of the year, when robust buying sent them to a peak of 130-150 U.S. cents over spot London prices.
Traders said the outlook for gold prices over the next few weeks and months remained gloomy.
"I see $328 as the next support level. It failed to hold at $340. That's a bad sign," one dealer said.
Another trader said there have been various estimates that gold will drop to $300 by the end of the year.
-- Rene Pastor in Singapore (65-8703305)
-- Mishi Saran in Hong Kong (852) 2843 6358
